title: Instruction Encoding and Assembly Programming
subtitle: From assembly text to the 32 bits the processor reads.

references.title: Instructions: Language of the Computer
references.topics: Representing instructions in the computer: MIPS instruction formats (R, I, J), fields, encoding and decoding; translating and starting a program

objectives: Explain the three MIPS instruction formats (R, I, J) and their fields
Encode an assembly instruction into 32-bit binary and hex
Decode a 32-bit word back into assembly
Read a machine-code listing, including branch offsets
Write and run a small assembly program

steps.question: Your processor never sees the text `add $s0, $s1, $s2`. What does it actually receive, and how does 32 bits say all of that?
clues: Groups of bits (fields) name the operation and each register.
Turning text into those bits is called **encoding**; reading them back is **decoding**.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: Assembly to machine code

nodes.label: Instruction format
nodes.note: The operation decides which fields exist.

steps.why: This is the translation an assembler does for every instruction of your program.
steps.real: The executable file on your computer is a long list of such 32-bit words.

explainAgain.beginner: Think of a form with boxes: the format says how many boxes there are and how wide each one is.

steps.title: R-type: register instructions
steps.why: R-type arithmetic, logical and shift instructions all share one layout; `funct` tells them apart.

mistake.wrong: rd is the first register in the machine code word.
mistake.right: In the word the order is rs, rt, rd, but the assembly writes the destination first.

notes.explain: Show `add $s0,$s1,$s2`: assembly order is rd, rs, rt; the word order is rs, rt, rd.

steps.title: I-type: immediates, loads, stores, branches
steps.why: The 16-bit field holds a constant, a memory offset or a branch offset, depending on the opcode.

steps.title: J-type: jumps
steps.why: A jump gives up the register fields to get 26 bits of address.

deeper.text: The 26-bit field is the target address shifted right by 2, because every instruction address is a multiple of 4.

steps.title: Look at the fields

blocks.title: The three formats
blocks.hint: Pick an R-type, an I-type and a J-type example and compare the colored fields.

steps.why: Notice that op, rs and rt sit in the same bit positions for R-type and I-type, which simplifies the hardware.

steps.question: Which format does `lw $t0, 8($s1)` use?
steps.why: Loads use the I-format: op, rs (base), rt (destination) and a 16-bit offset.
feedback: R-type instructions have a funct field and use three registers.
J-type has only an opcode and a 26-bit target.

steps.title: Encoding step by step

items: **1.** Choose the format from the instruction (R, I or J)
**2.** Look up the opcode (and funct for R-type)
**3.** Convert each register name to its number
**4.** Place every value in its field, padded to the field width
**6.** Group the bits in fours to write hex

steps.why: This is exactly what an assembler does, billions of times over a large program.
steps.real: A compiler produces assembly; an assembler produces these words.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement about encoding is wrong. Click it.
lines: 1. add, sub and slt are all R-type with opcode 0.
2. The funct field selects the operation inside R-type.
3. lw and sw have the same opcode.
4. The 16-bit immediate of an I-type instruction is sign-extended.
steps.explain: lw has opcode 35 and sw has opcode 43.
steps.fix: lw uses opcode 35; sw uses opcode 43.

questions.q: How many fields does an R-type instruction have and what are they?
questions.a: Six: op, rs, rt, rd, shamt and funct (6, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6 bits).

questions.q: Which bits hold a branch offset?
questions.a: The 16-bit immediate field of the I-format, counted in instructions.
It selects the operation among R-type instructions.

steps.title: Decoding: read the opcode first

nodes.label: Opcode
nodes.note: Zero means R-type: look at funct. 2 or 3 means J-type. Anything else is I-type.

nodes.label: Fields
nodes.note: Cut the 32 bits at the format's boundaries.

nodes.label: Assembly
nodes.note: Put the registers back in assembly order.

steps.why: The processor does this decoding in hardware in every single instruction cycle.
steps.real: A disassembler or debugger does the same job to show you assembly for a program that has none.

steps.question: Decode `0x01095020`. Which instruction is it?
steps.result: The destination is rd = $t2, printed first.

steps.title: Try it: decode a word
steps.why: Decoding is encoding run backwards.

steps.question: Decode `0x8D090004`.
steps.why: Opcode 35 is lw; rs = 8 ($t0) is the base, rt = 9 ($t1) is the destination, offset 4.
feedback: rs and rt are swapped here: rs is the base.

steps.question: The 16-bit immediate field of an instruction is `1111 1111 1111 1111`. As a signed number what is it?
steps.why: All ones in two's complement is −1.
feedback: 65,535 is the unsigned reading; the immediate is sign-extended.

steps.statement: Two different instructions can have the same opcode but different funct fields.
steps.why: All R-type instructions have opcode 0 and are told apart by funct.

steps.title: From program to machine-code listing
steps.why: The assembler gives each instruction an address, and branch offsets count instructions from the next address.
steps.real: This table is what a disassembler shows when you look at a program.

mistake.wrong: The loop label is stored in the branch instruction.
mistake.right: Labels disappear. The branch holds an offset: here −3 instructions.

notes.explain: Point at the bne word 0x1520FFFD: the low 16 bits 0xFFFD are −3. The label loop is at 0x00400008; bne is at 0x00400010.

steps.title: Run it: the same program

blocks.title: Sum 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1
blocks.program:
addi $t0, $zero, 0
addi $t1, $zero, 5
loop: add $t0, $t0, $t1
addi $t1, $t1, -1
bne $t1, $zero, loop
blocks.hint: Step through. $t0 collects the sum while $t1 counts down.

steps.why: The listing above is exactly what the processor fetches and executes.

steps.question: What will `$t0` hold when the loop above finishes?
steps.result: The loop adds the counter to the sum until the counter reaches 0.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Why do all MIPS instructions have the same length (32 bits) even though some need fewer fields?
steps.answer: A fixed length makes fetching and decoding simple and fast: the next instruction is always 4 bytes ahead, and the fields are always in the same place. The price is some unused bits, which is a deliberate compromise.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: MIPS uses three formats. What would you gain and lose with one format only, or with ten?
ideas: One format is simplest for the hardware but wastes bits (no room for 26-bit jump targets and 16-bit immediates).
Ten formats would use every bit well, but decoding becomes slower and more complex.
Three formats keep the opcode, rs and rt in similar places.

steps.question: List the fields of the R-type format with their widths.
steps.answer: op 6, rs 5, rt 5, rd 5, shamt 5, funct 6 bits.

steps.question: Encode `add $t2, $s0, $s1` in hex.
steps.hint: Remember the word order is rs, rt, rd.
steps.mistake: Putting the destination first in the machine word.

steps.question: Decode `0x00A63820`.
steps.solution: op 0 means R-type. rs = 5 ($a1), rt = 6 ($a2), rd = 7 ($a3), funct 0x20 = add.
steps.hint: Write the word in binary and cut it at 6, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6 bits.

steps.question: Encode `lw $s1, 16($t0)` and say which register is rs.
steps.hint: In the I-format rs is the base and rt is the register loaded.

steps.question: The 32 bits are 100011 01001 01000 0000000000001100. Write the instruction.
steps.mistake: Swapping the base and destination registers.

steps.title: Exam practice: jump

steps.question: Explain why MIPS has R, I and J formats instead of one format.
steps.answer: One format cannot give each instruction what it needs: R-type needs three registers and a function code, I-type needs a 16-bit constant or offset, and jumps need a 26-bit address. Three formats keep every instruction 32 bits and keep the first fields in the same place, balancing simplicity against the bits each instruction needs.
steps.solution: A strong answer names the fields each format needs and the fixed-length compromise.
steps.mistake: Saying the formats exist only for speed.
steps.title: Exam practice: conceptual
What you should remember
remember: Every MIPS instruction is one 32-bit word.
R-type: op, rs, rt, rd, shamt, funct (6, 5, 5, 5, 5, 6 bits); opcode 0, funct picks the operation.
I-type: op, rs, rt, 16-bit immediate (constant, offset or branch offset).
J-type: op and a 26-bit word address (byte address divided by 4).
Encode: pick format, look up op/funct, convert registers, fill fields, join, write hex.
Decode by reading the opcode first, then splitting the word.

mistakes.wrong: The destination register comes first in the machine word.
mistakes.right: The word order is rs, rt, rd; assembly writes the destination first.

mistakes.wrong: The branch instruction stores the label.
mistakes.right: It stores an offset in instructions from PC + 4.

mistakes.wrong: Jump targets store the full byte address.
mistakes.right: They store the address divided by 4.

mistakes.wrong: All R-type instructions have different opcodes.
mistakes.right: They all have opcode 0 and differ in funct.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: An assembler turns each instruction into one 32-bit word using one of three formats. R-type holds three registers and a function code, I-type holds two registers and a 16-bit immediate, J-type holds a 26-bit address. Encoding fills those fields from lookup tables, decoding reads the opcode first, and branch offsets count instructions from the next one.

questions.question: How many bits is a MIPS instruction?
questions.misconception: Fixed length is one of the RISC design choices.

questions.statement: In R-type instructions the opcode is always 0.
questions.why: The funct field selects the operation.
questions.misconception: Opcode 0 only tells you to look at funct.

questions.question: What is the hex word for `add $s0, $s1, $s2`?
What does `0x2129FFFF` decode to?
questions.why: Opcode 8 is addi; both registers are $t1 (9); the immediate 0xFFFF is −1.
questions.misconception: The immediate is sign-extended, so all ones means −1.

questions.question: A `beq` at 0x00400020 targets 0x00400030. What offset is stored?
questions.misconception: Count from the next instruction in instructions, not bytes.

questions.question: What is the 26-bit target field when `j` goes to 0x00400100?
Which instruction has opcode 43?
questions.why: 43 is the opcode of sw (lw is 35).
questions.misconception: Stores and loads have different opcodes.

questions.question: In the listing, `bne $t1,$zero,loop` sits at 0x00400010 and `loop` is at 0x00400008. Which statement is true?
options: The immediate field is −3 instructions from PC + 4
The immediate field stores the label name
The immediate field stores the byte address of the label
questions.why: The target is 2 instructions before the bne’s own position, i.e. 3 before PC + 4, so the offset is −3.
questions.misconception: The offset is relative to PC + 4 and signed.

items.q: List the R-type fields and widths.
items.a: op 6, rs 5, rt 5, rd 5, shamt 5, funct 6.

items.q: What do you read first when decoding?
How is a jump target stored?
items.a: As the 26-bit word address (byte address divided by 4).

items.q: What does a branch offset count?
items.a: Instructions, from the instruction after the branch.
